« On n’est pas tous des voleurs » – à Ri: “We’re not all thieves” – in Rivière-des-Prairies, teens are screened outside Dollarama
À Rivière-des-Prairies, des élèves du se: In Rivière-des-Prairies, high school students are let into Dollarama two at a time. A legal scholar sees discrimination.
Cet article est né d’un exercice réalisé: This article grew out of an exercise by teenagers from Rivière-des-Prairies, part of a training in vertical journalism for Instagram that La Converse offered at the request of Le Phare, an organization that works with young people in the neighbourhood.
Lors d’une séance de remue-méninges sur: During a brainstorming session on the issues that concern them in their daily lives, the teens raised the restrictions on student access at certain businesses in the area, notably outside a Dollarama near Jean-Grou secondary school. La Converse then suggested they do a vox pop on the situation as part of their training exercise.
Les témoignages recueillis ont ensuite c: The testimonies they gathered then led our newsroom to dig deeper into the subject independently. We sought to determine whether the practice observed in Rivière-des-Prairies was an isolated case or part of a broader phenomenon. Among other things, this meant examining similar cases documented elsewhere in Quebec since 2016, asking Dollarama for an explanation, and interviewing law professor Louis-Philippe Lampron about the scope of this practice with regard to the right to equality and the Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms.
La formation offerte à l’organisme Le Ph: The training offered to Le Phare was therefore the starting point for the story, but the article was conceived, researched and produced independently by La Converse.
<strong>À l’heure du dîner, des dizaines: At lunchtime, dozens of students from Jean-Grou secondary school in Rivière-des-Prairies line up outside the neighbourhood Dollarama to buy something to eat. For about three years now, they have only been allowed in two at a time. The scene repeats itself in the heat and in the cold. For a law professor consulted by La Converse, the practice amounts, based on the facts reported, to age-based discrimination.
Il est midi passé, boulevard Perras à Ri: It’s just past noon on Perras Boulevard in Rivière-des-Prairies. About thirty students from Jean-Grou secondary school are lined up outside the neighbourhood Dollarama. The sun is at its peak on this June day, and the heat weighs on the teenagers. Entry into the store is screened by a security guard. The young people are allowed in, but only two at a time. Inside, chocolate bars, chips and sugary drinks for less than $5 – most of what many of them can afford before heading back to class.
Depuis l’ouverture du magasin, il y a en: Since the store opened about five years ago, this scene has played out every school day, rain or shine. For many of the teens we met, the restriction sends a clear message: they are seen as a threat before they even step through the door. Yet as Eyana points out: “We’re literally customers like everyone else. We come to pay.”
Le temps d’attente varie selon les jours: The wait varies from day to day. Natalia says she stays outside the store about ten minutes when she arrives early, but up to half an hour when the line is longer. “Especially when the weather’s extreme, when it’s too hot or too cold, I find it’s pointless,” she says. “It’s a waste of time.” For her classmate Eyana, the wait can be even longer. “With a line like that, you can wait 30 minutes or more. Some people wait an hour.” Zoé says some students sometimes end up late for school.
Mais le temps passé à attendre dehors n’: But the time spent waiting outside isn’t what bothers them most. When asked why they think they’re subject to this restriction, their answers often come back to the same idea: by adopting this measure, the store is trying to prevent theft and the disruptions that some students might cause.
C’est cette raison que les jeunes contes: It’s this reasoning that the teens contest. “Anyone can steal,” Eyana continues. “Adults can steal just as much as kids. It’s not up to us to suffer the consequences for those who steal.”
Laurianne décrit le malaise autrement. P: Laurianne describes the discomfort differently. For her, lining up outside while adults walk in normally feels like being publicly singled out as a problem. “It’s like a humiliation in front of everybody,” she says. “Adults can go in, but we can’t.” Tristan also feels that young people are treated as suspects before they’ve even done anything. “They should give us a chance to prove to them that we don’t steal.”
Plusieurs élèves racontent devoir égalem: Several students say they also have to leave their bags before going in and feel watched once inside the store. Zoé makes a direct link to the backgrounds of many of the young people who attend the school and frequent the businesses in the area. “I think it’s because we’re Black and Arab and they’re scared we’ll steal,” she adds. She isn’t claiming that nobody steals. But, she insists, just because some do doesn’t mean everyone else should be treated the same way.
Le sentiment exprimé par ces jeunes ne p: The feeling expressed by these young people cannot, on its own, lead to a legal conclusion of racial profiling. But it adds to another finding that is more easily observable: here, the restriction targets a specific group – high school students.
Wesley connaît bien le secteur. Interven: Wesley knows the area well. A youth worker with Équipe RDP’s young leaders program, he regularly walks through what he calls the commercial hub around the school. His role includes preventing tensions and stepping in when a situation risks escalating. He says he has seen lines form outside the Dollarama for years.
Il ne met pas en doute le fait que le co: He doesn’t doubt that the store may have experienced theft or disruptions. But for him, the solution chosen to address the problem is hard to justify. “It’s not true that out of 60 students, all 60 are necessarily coming to steal,” he says. In his view, other approaches could have been favoured, notably more staff or security guards inside the store.
Wesley reconnaît toutefois qu’un commerc: Wesley acknowledges, however, that a store of that size can hardly take in dozens of teenagers arriving at the same time. “Sure, it’s complicated if 60 kids start walking into the Dollarama every time [...] But at the same time, leaving the kids outside like that, especially in winter, it’s not great.”
La Converse a demandé à Dollarama si la: La Converse asked Dollarama whether the restriction imposed on Jean-Grou students was a local or regional decision, or whether it came from the company’s head office. We also asked what losses or disruptions had prompted the measure, whether any data existed, and whether less restrictive solutions had been considered.
L’entreprise n’a pas répondu à toutes no: The company did not answer all of our questions. In its written response, Lyla Radmanovich, Dollarama’s media relations manager, instead explains that “entrance control is one of the measures used across [our] Canadian network, and for several years, to ensure the safety of our premises, prevent losses and support the smooth running of operations.” The company specifies that this measure can be used when a large number of customers arrive at the same time. M<sup>s</sup>. Radmanovich then adds: “When it is put in place, it must apply to all customers.”
Or, c’est précisément cela qui ne corres: Yet that is precisely what does not match the scene observed outside the Rivière-des-Prairies store on June 9. At lunchtime, adults were going in normally. Jean-Grou students, for their part, were lining up and being admitted two at a time under the watch of a security guard.
Sur place, le gérant avait confirmé à La: On site, the manager had confirmed to La Converse that students had caused disruptions at lunchtime in the past. He also explained that the presence of a security guard, for about two years, made it possible to manage the situation without pulling store employees away from their tasks. The head office’s response thus contrasts with what was observed on site, where the restriction applies to Jean-Grou students.
« Ça, c’est la définition même de la dis: “That is the very definition of age-based discrimination in this context and in access to public places,” says Professor Louis-Philippe Lampron. “That’s basic, straightforward discrimination.”
En entrevue avec La Converse, le profess: In an interview with La Converse, Professor Lampron, who teaches the course Human Rights and Freedoms at Université Laval, specifies that only a court could rule on a discrimination case. But based on the facts reported to him, he believes there would be a good chance of demonstrating, in the Rivière-des-Prairies case, a violation of the right to equality, which is protected by the Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms.
Pour lui, l’argument de la gestion de l’: In his view, the crowd-management argument doesn’t hold up if only young people are targeted, because, he continues, a business can perfectly well limit the number of people inside. But that rule must then apply regardless of age. In the case reported by La Converse, the measure would therefore not be neutral. “Here, since there’s a criterion based on age, the policy is not neutral at all. It discriminates against people,” he says.
Par ailleurs, l’existence de vols ou de: Moreover, the existence of theft or problematic behaviour is not enough, in his view, to impose an access restriction on an entire group. “That’s the whole purpose of the right to equality,” he continues. A business may have good reasons to want to ensure its security or prevent losses. But it must still be able to justify the means it chooses. In his words, “there are ways to solve the crowding problem without introducing discriminatory criteria.”
Louis-Philippe Lampron considère que, po: Louis-Philippe Lampron considers that, for students who feel they are victims of such a practice, the Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse (CDPDJ), Quebec’s human rights and youth rights commission, is the most appropriate avenue. It can investigate a situation, try to reach an agreement with the business or, if necessary, bring the case before the Human Rights Tribunal.
<strong>Dix ans plus tard, le problème c: Ten years later, the problem changes address
Les files sur le boulevard Perras ne con: The lines on Perras Boulevard are not isolated cases. For at least 10 years, similar situations have been documented in Quebec, often near high schools. The places change, the students change, but the reasons given and the restrictions imposed look alike.
En 2016, des élèves de l’école secondair: In 2016, students at Jeanne-Mance secondary school in Montréal had denounced restrictions imposed at several businesses near their school. At a Dollarama on Mont-Royal Avenue, young people had to wait before being allowed in, while other customers could enter the store normally.
À la suite du dépôt d’une plainte par un: After a student filed a complaint, Dollarama ended the practice at that location. The CDPDJ then said it had already received several complaints about similar restrictions targeting young people. Most striking is that, at the time, the company was already defending entrance controls by explaining that the measure targeted “no particular segment of the population.”
Dix ans plus tard, dans sa réponse à La: Ten years later, in its response to La Converse, Dollarama again states that entrance controls can be used to regulate crowds, while specifying that the measure must apply to all customers.
Entre les deux, en 2020, un adolescent d: In between, in 2020, a teenager in Québec City had denounced an almost identical practice at a Dollarama in his neighbourhood. Young people there were subject to an access restriction that did not apply to adults. The company then justified the measure as a way to prevent theft, before committing to review it. Then, in December 2025, the same approach reappeared in Verdun, where high school students were screened at several businesses near their school.
D’un cas à l’autre, le même scénario sem: From one case to the next, the same scenario seems to repeat: a practice is denounced locally, a debate begins and, sometimes, the measure is changed. A few years later, somewhere else, teenagers again say they are being screened at the entrance to a store.
Louis-Philippe Lampron ne prétend pas co: Louis-Philippe Lampron does not claim to know the outcome of every case or whether each publicized situation led to a complaint to the human rights commission. He nonetheless believes this repetition deserves examination. “The fact that it keeps happening suggests to me that there may be something to clarify here,” he says.
Le 9 juin dernier, boulevard Perras, cet: On June 9, on Perras Boulevard, this repetition took the form of a line of about thirty teenagers waiting in the sun. Some found the wait simply annoying. Others spoke of discrimination. Still others acknowledged that some students may have caused problems, while refusing to be associated with them.
Tous, cependant, attendaient devant la m: All of them, however, were waiting at the same door. Ten years after the first publicized cases, the practice continues to be adopted. It has changed schools, neighbourhoods and students, but at the door of the stores, the suspicion remains the same.
À Rivière-des-Prairies, les élèves de l': In Rivière-des-Prairies, students from Jean-Grou secondary school can only enter the neighbourhood Dollarama two at a time, a practice that has been in place for years. A law professor at Université Laval sees age-based discrimination, while Dollarama cites crowd management — a justification already challenged in similar cases in Montréal, Québec City and Verdun over the past ten years.
